You are here Step 9 of 9, Maintain · 9.1 Maintain Eligibility

Mom's Medicaid Letters and Dates in One Place

What arrived, what it asks for, and where it's kept.

Download PDF

The approval notice is in a folder, the second letter is in your sister's purse, and the renewal date is on a page nobody can find.

This page doesn't ask you to understand any of it. It asks what has arrived, the date on it, what it asks for, where it is and who has it.

The letters

One line per letter. In the third column, copy the letter's own words.

Letter from the Medicaid agencyThe date on itWhat it asks for, and any date it givesWhere it's kept, and who has it
The approval notice, every page
Any letter that mentions a renewal or a review
Any letter that asks the family to send or do something
Any letter about a change in Mom's coverage
Anything about her Medicaid that went to a care facility's business office instead of to the family

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What goes in the folder with them

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it
Copies of anything the family has sent to the agency, with the date sent
The Medicaid agency's phone number, and any caseworker's name
Mom's bank and other account statements since the application
Her legal and financial documents
The calendar where the dates from the letters are written
Contact details for your Medicaid planner and any other professional helping

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Any line above with nothing beside it, and any date you expected to find and didn't, such as the next renewal. Put a name next to each.

For example No letter mentions a renewal date. Karen will ask the caseworker on Monday.

How to use it

  • Write each date exactly as the letter prints it. If a letter has no date, write “undated” and keep its envelope with it.
  • Don't rewrite or sum up a letter here. Copy what it asks for and say where it is.
  • Where a letter gives a date, put that date on the calendar as well.
  • Bring this page and the folder to any conversation with the Medicaid agency or your Medicaid planner.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any letter means, what has to be sent, or when. The agency's own notices are the authority on dates and requirements. If you read something you don't understand, that's a question for the office that sent it, or for your Medicaid planner. Nothing here is legal, financial or tax advice.

Where this comes from

Keeping every letter from the agency follows the federal renewal flyer for people with Medicaid, which says to watch the mail. The rows come from the Medicaid Planning Roadmap's working list for this step.
